sentences.text: Noasaurus leali is the only known species of this small theropod dinosaur.
While Gregory S. Paul estimated its length at 1.5 meters and weight at 15 kilograms, a 2024 study based on skull and metatarsal dimensions suggested lengths between 1.6 and 2 meters.

The skull anatomy remains poorly known because only a left maxilla and a right quadrate are preserved, though the animal possessed ziphodont teeth that were laterally compressed, recurved, and serrated on both edges.
Comparisons with related dinosaurs and the elongation of its known neck bones suggest Noasaurus likely had a long, S-shaped neck.
Curved claws initially thought to be foot claws were later identified as belonging to the forelimbs, resembling those of spinosaurids and possibly used to catch fish.
The holotype specimen PVL 4061 was discovered in April 1975 in the Lecho Formation of Southern Salta by a team led by Professor José F. Bonaparte.
Recovered materials from the site included remains of at least five sauropod individuals, including the titanosaur Saltasaurus loricatus.

A cervical vertebra found at the site was initially identified in 1999 as oviraptorosaurian, suggesting a rare presence of that group in Gondwana, but in 2007 it was re-identified as belonging to Noasaurus.
Bonaparte and Powell formally named and described the species Noasaurus leali in 1980.
Researchers suggest Noasaurus was an opportunistic mesopredator that likely fed on small vertebrates and fish.
In 2004, one of the hand claws was re-identified as belonging to the hand rather than the foot.
Bonaparte and Powell originally assigned Noasaurus to its own family, the Noasauridae, but the genus is currently classified as a member of the Ceratosauria.
Noasaurus lived during the late Cretaceous period, approximately 70 million years ago between the Campanian and Maastrichtian stages, in what is now South America.
The environment where Noasaurus lived was a coastal plain with ponds and lagoons that likely supported a tropical coastal forest in a hot, humid environment near the Tropic of Capricorn.

There was a debate over whether the large curved claws belonged to the feet or hands, with later studies confirming they were hand claws. Paul hypothesized that noasaurines were South American counterparts of dromaeosaurids through convergent evolution, a view later undermined by the discovery that the claws were on the hands. Paul also hypothesized that Noasaurus might have used a kicking technique to disembowel prey due to short forelimbs, assuming it used foot claws like dromaeosaurids, but this was disproven when the claws were identified as hand claws.
In 2024, Hendrickx et al. placed Noasaurus in a polytomy with other small noasaurids, suggesting a radiation of small-bodied forms during the Late Cretaceous.
